Sometime in about 2009 or so, I was working a closing shift at a subway in an automall. I closed down at 6 and spent a few minutes bullshitting with the gas station attendant. Unfortunately this ended up making me miss my bus.

It was pissing rain, which is normal for the PNW. But this was an intense downpour. Within minutes I gave up on staying dry. I put all my important stuff in my inside pocket to keep it dryish and just allowed the rain to soak through.

Depressed and angry I stood there waiting on the bus. Finally, it arrived on the other side of the street. I considered walking across and climbing on. But it was just about to do a short look before coming back to me. Well two people got off the bus and started crossing the street before noticing me. They started to approach and say something. But as I was listening to my head phones I couldn't hear him at first. Also this was a rather sketchy part of town known for its transients. So I pulled off my head phones with one hand and stuck my hand in my pocket to ready my knife if necessary. Well the dude was just wanting to bum a smoke. I hooked him up and we just kind of idly chatted about the rain.

As they were about to head off, I inquired about if they knew of a dry spot to smoke some pot. After my shift and the rain. I just wanted to relax and roast and set my mind at ease.

They responded that they had a camp set up not far from where we were and that I could smoke there.

Well, I was a bit sketched out. And actually responded "okay, but don't go and murder me." to which they laughed and requested the same courtesy.

So we walked several blocks up the road, past the car dealerships and into newer and newer commercial buildings, until the buildings ceased and the road dead ended at a forest. From there we wandered into the forest along some almost non-existent trail. It was pitch black and stormy, with nothing but our little flashlights to illuminate the way. There was a bit of slipping and sliding, but otherwise the trip was uneventful.

We finally made it to their tent and got inside. It was a spacious living space, there was the main room with a bed area in the back and then a small room connected to the side where their room mate lived. The whole thing was carved into the side of a ravine. He had excavated about 10 feet into the side and leveled it all out. Their bed was built on an elevated part of the dirt. All in all it was the best camp I had ever seen. So after arriving and taking off our sopping wet costs and what not. I finally got to properly meet my hosts.

Karma and his girl Phoenix were their names. And over a few bowls we talked and I got to know them.

Karma (the guy), is someone I'll never forget. He had a tragic past that just broke my heart learning about. He was an orphan who was never adopted. So after 14 years at the orphanage, when it became apparent no one would adopt him. He became a ward of the state. I don't know the rules of state he grew up. But instead of some sort of foster home. They sent him juvenile jail. This young man who had done nothing but be unwanted was punished in jail. He was put in with arsonists, drug addicts, thugs and abusers. This was the population that taught him about life. Karma learned to fight at an early age because he had to to defend himself. He was forced to associate and live with these criminals. It was the only life he knew, but he knew it was wrong.

Why was he being punished? Jail is for those who committed a crime. And what crime did he commit? Misty eyed, he described his ordeal world. In which if this had to happen, then there should be a separate part of the jail for cases like his. Perhaps fenced off from the rest of the population and given more privileges. As these kids were here because of a dumb system, not as a form of punishment.

After he turned 18. He was not quite capable of willing to live what most would call a normal life. He determined he would never pay taxes to the fucked up system that had punished him all his life.

He began his travels then. Hitching and train hopping from place to place. Seeing sunsets above oceans, sunrises from the peaks of mountains. Thunderstorms over the rolling planes. He supported himself with odd jobs for people where he got paid directly from them. Or just panhandling.

I had this misconception that all homeless people were unhappy with their circumstances. However karma is one of the happiest and most content people I've ever met. He proved me wrong and shattered this misconception.

We talked for about two hours as our combined body heat started to warm the tent up. We smoked and joked and talked. It was very refreshing. As I was preparing to leave to catch my bus I decided to impart some gifts.

Karma's knuckles were broken repeatedly over the years and by this point were rather mangled. He also smoked hand rolled cigarettes. Which I had witnessed him struggle with while his fingers were cold and numb. I had one of the cheap manual cigarette rollers that I used for joints. I decided then and there, that he needed it much more then I. I also gave them my foot long sandwich I made from work and a bowl of chili.

I also hid $20 under their pillow when they weren't looking.

I then had them escort me through the forest back to civilisation. When we arrived back at the street, I also gifted them my flashlight. It wasn't much, but they only had the one between the two of them.

That was almost seven years ago now. And I still think about them occasionally. He taught me a few things that I've always kept with my. And I'll never forget him.

In the south west united states, in a place that I still struggle to understand why anyone settled there. The desert is hell. You guys know that right?

Anyway, there was a spanish/native homeless fellow. 45-50 years old and pretty rough. He asked me for something. Now, I figured it was the usual, "just a couple bucks?", coming from a person who didn't actually need a couple bucks. Like +90% of the time.

I started to do the make eye-contact and shake my head or blank them without speaking thing. When I saw him though, I saw sincerity.

I asked him what he said again. Turns out he was asking for a coat. That was a first. A fucking coat! I looked at the sky, still suspicious but that was fading as fast as the storm that was moving in.

I asked him to wait, and went to my vehicle. I brought him a hooded cotton/fleece jacket. He didn't have a single thing but the clothes on his back. No bag, no scarf, no smokes, no food or drink. Nothing.

He said that his daughter was in the AF and he hadn't seen her in years. That he had to sell his car, to make rent on an apartment he lost anyway. He didn't say it in a bleating, appealing manner. More of a quiet resignation and lament. Not long. Sincere.

Don't get me wrong, He was clearly a drunk, and that was probably why he was out there. But, it was like, he shouldn't be. Like some people bring everything onto themselves, and others just can't handle as much and break. He was the second kind.

His eyes welled up as he talked about his daughter. He wanted to visit her but couldn't. Too far.

This all took place at a gas station. I hugged him and went inside to conduct my business. While inside I thought about him and the desert.

I went back to my vehicle to get a bag, food, water, lighter, trash bags and a pack of cigarettes for him. I had plenty, and the desert is cruel.

He was gone though. Not hanging around begging from others.

Just needed a coat.

(I'm aware he may have been just a brilliant story teller/beggar...but a coat? And even if that is the case...His acting earned the damn thing.)
